name: Pattern 7: Speech as a Bridge
title: Pattern 7: Speech as a Bridge
answer: Speech as a Bridge is the seventh of ten patterns that recur across AI in schools: speech technology gives students a way around a barrier so they can reach the same content as everyone else. Text to speech reads a page aloud, speech to text lets a student say what they know, and live captions keep deaf, hard of hearing and English learner students in the lesson. It matters because access and skill building are separate questions, and the team around the student, not the software, decides which one applies.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern uses speech tools to open doors that print and writing can close. Text to speech reads a page aloud for a student who struggles with print, while speech to text lets a student with a writing disability speak their answer instead of writing it. Live captions serve students who are deaf or hard of hearing and also help English learners keep up with a fast lecture. Tools such as Microsoft Immersive Reader gather several of these supports into one place. The problem it solves is that a student can understand a subject yet be blocked from showing it by the medium the school uses.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In preschool and the early grades, speech tools appear as read aloud practice and fluency feedback. The book urges patience at this stage, because a six week study of an AI voice tutor with children aged 3 to 7 found the tool ran the literacy activities as consistently as parents did, yet children learned more when a parent read with them. The tool also had trouble understanding young children's speech, so a parent or teacher still had to listen closely. In later grades the same tools support access to content, captions in lectures and spoken responses in place of written ones. Across all grades the choice of when to use the bridge and when to build the skill is made per student.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this pattern's evidence with a call for patience in the early grades. A six week study of an AI voice tutor with children aged 3 to 7 found that it delivered the literacy activities as consistently as parents did, but children learned more when a parent read with them (Quan et al., 2026). The same study found the tool struggled to understand young children's speech, so a parent or teacher still had to listen closely. On the question of access versus skill, researchers describe strategic offloading: using the tool for access while still teaching the skill the tool replaces (Seung & Basham, 2026).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The central limit is that a bridge is not a substitute for teaching the skill it bypasses. A student with a reading disability may need text to speech to learn history, but may also need direct reading instruction without it, and the book frames this as strategic offloading rather than a permanent replacement. The individualized education program team, not the software, decides which is which for each student. In the early grades the tool's difficulty understanding young children's speech means an adult still has to listen closely. These decisions stay with people, and nothing here is legal advice.
